mainTopic: Does יאוש make a thief the owner? Challenges from both sides, and רב יוסף's rule that a change in name counts like a physical change.
overview: This amud asks whether an owner's giving up hope (יאוש) makes a thief the owner of what he stole. רב יוסף challenges רבה with the case of stolen חמץ after פסח. רבה answers that יאוש works only when the thief wants the item, and nobody wants forbidden חמץ. אביי then challenges רבה from the word קרבנו, which excludes a stolen animal. רבא answers that the ברייתא can be about an animal that was already a קרבן when it was stolen. Next אביי challenges רב יוסף from a משנה in which a thief's or robber's decision about hides makes them able to become impure. That would show יאוש קונה. רב יוסף first answers that the hides were trimmed, but רבה בר רב חנן shows that a table-top cover needs no trimming. So רבא reports רב יוסף's final answer: a change in name counts like a physical change. The גמרא then challenges this from a stolen beam built into a building, where the owner gets money only because of תקנת השבים.

steps.title: The stolen חמץ case: why may the thief just hand it back?
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף points out that once פסח arrives the owner surely gives up hope on his חמץ. If יאוש gave the thief ownership, the thief should owe full money and not be allowed to just return the worthless bread.
steps.simpleTranslation: The thief may say to him: "Here is yours in front of you." But in this case, once the time of the prohibition arrives, the owner surely gives up hope. If you think יאוש makes the thief the owner, why can he say "Here is yours in front of you"? He should have to pay him full, proper money!
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף finishes quoting a ruling about a thief who stole חמץ and then פסח passed. He uses it to attack רבה's view that יאוש makes the thief the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling lets the thief return the useless חמץ as is. But when פסח came, the owner certainly gave up hope on it. If יאוש made the thief the owner, then the חמץ became the thief's own. He would then owe the owner its value in good money, not worthless bread.

keyTerms.meaning: The owner giving up hope of getting his item back
Giving up hope makes the thief the owner
"Here is yours in front of you": returning the item as it is now, without paying for any loss in value
The time the prohibition starts (here, when חמץ becomes forbidden on פסח)
Full, proper money

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two ways a thief can repay. Returning the item itself ("here is yours") is allowed only if it still belongs to the owner. If the thief became the owner through יאוש, he would owe its value in money instead.

phrases.english: He says to him: "Here is yours in front of you."
But in this case, once the time of the prohibition has arrived,
the owner certainly gives up hope;
and if you think that giving up hope makes the thief the owner,
why may he say to him: "Here is yours in front of you"?
He should have to pay him full, proper money!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ יֵאוּשׁ קוֹנֶה, אַמַּאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב יוסף's objection to רבה's earlier claim that יאוש קונה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's rule that יאוש makes the thief the owner
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Once פסח came, יאוש certainly happened. If יאוש gave ownership, the חמץ would be the thief's and he would owe its value. Yet the law lets him return it as is, so יאוש must not give ownership.

steps.title: יאוש only gives ownership when the thief wants to own the item
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that יאוש makes the thief the owner only when the thief wants to own the item. Nobody wants forbidden חמץ, so the thief never becomes its owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: When I say that יאוש gives ownership, I mean when the owner gives up hope and the thief wants to own it. Here, the owner gives up hope but the thief does not want to own it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה defends his rule by adding a condition: the thief has to want to own the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Ownership needs two sides: the owner lets go through יאוש, and the thief wants to take it. Forbidden חמץ is worthless, so the thief has no wish to own it. It stays the owner's, and the thief can return it as is. רבה's basic rule that יאוש קונה stays in place.

keyTerms.meaning: Gives up hope
Wants to own it
"When I said it, I meant...": a speaker explaining the limits of his own earlier statement

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that, according to רבה, יאוש alone is not enough. The thief must also want to own the item, and that limits where his rule applies.

phrases.english: He said to him: When I say it,
phrases.notes: This is רבה answering רב יוסף.

phrases.english: I mean where this one gives up hope and that one wants to own it;
here, this one gives up hope
but that one does not want to own it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's objection from step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the rule: it applies only when the thief wants to own the item
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יאוש alone always makes the thief the owner, even of forbidden חמץ
steps.terutzMaskana: יאוש gives ownership only together with the thief's wish to own. Forbidden חמץ is something nobody wants, so it stays the owner's.

steps.title: אביי cites "his offering, not a stolen one" and rules out the case before יאוש
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבה with a ברייתא: the word קרבנו excludes a stolen animal. That cannot be talking about before יאוש, because then no פסוק would be needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי challenged רבה: "His offering," and not a stolen one. What is the case? If you say it is before יאוש, why do I need a פסוק? That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי opens a new challenge to רבה from a ברייתא about stolen offerings. He sets up his argument by ruling out the first possible case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before יאוש the animal clearly still belongs to the owner. A thief obviously cannot bring someone else's animal as his own offering, so the פסוק would be teaching nothing new. This prepares the next step: the ברייתא must be talking about after יאוש.

keyTerms.meaning: "His offering": the offering must belong to the one bringing it
The stolen item
What is the case?
It's obvious! (so no פסוק is needed)

phrases.english: אביי challenged רבה:
"His offering," and not a stolen one.
What is the case?
If you say it is before the owner gives up hope,
why do I need a פסוק? That's obvious!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבה answered רב יוסף, אביי brings a new and separate challenge to the same rule.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק excludes a stolen animal. Before יאוש this would be obvious, so the פסוק must be about after יאוש. That would show the thief still does not own it.

steps.title: So the ברייתא is after יאוש, which proves that יאוש does not give ownership
steps.stepSummary: אביי concludes that the ברייתא must be talking about after יאוש. Even then the thief may not offer the animal, so יאוש does not make him the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, isn't it talking about after יאוש? Learn from this that יאוש does not give ownership!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי finishes his argument. Since the case cannot be before יאוש, it must be after, and the thief still cannot offer it, which goes against רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If יאוש made the thief the owner, the animal would truly be "his offering" and he could bring it. The פסוק still calls it stolen and excludes it. This suggests the thief does not own it even after יאוש, which is a direct challenge to רבה.

keyTerms.meaning: "Rather, isn't it...?": pushing toward the only remaining option
After the owner gives up hope
Learn from this
Does not give ownership

steps.whatToRemember: אביי argues from the word קרבנו: if a stolen animal is still excluded after יאוש, then the thief never became its owner, so יאוש לא קני.

phrases.english: Rather, isn't it talking about after the owner gives up hope?
Learn from this that giving up hope does not make the thief the owner!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא לָאו לְאַחַר יֵאוּשׁ? שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ יֵאוּשׁ לָא קָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes אביי's challenge that began in step 3 by taking the only option left.
steps.raayaObject: That יאוש does not make the thief the owner (against רבה)
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא reading קרבנו to exclude a stolen animal, which must be talking about after יאוש

steps.title: רבא points to a parallel case about stolen bedding
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers אביי with 'by your logic': there is a similar ברייתא that says a זב's stolen bedding does not count as 'his bedding.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to אביי: According to your reasoning, what about the ברייתא that says the פסוק's words 'his bedding' leave out stolen bedding?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts to take apart אביי's proof by bringing a similar ברייתא. This line sets up a question that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי read 'קרבנו' as proof that even after יאוש a stolen animal is not the thief's. רבא brings a ברייתא with the same kind of wording, 'משכבו – ולא הגזול.' He is about to show that this kind of wording does not have to be about יאוש at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And according to your reasoning: turning the other person's logic back on him
His bedding: the bedding of a זָב, which can become impure
A man with a certain bodily discharge that makes him impure
The stolen item

phrases.english: Rava said to him:
And according to your reasoning,
that which is taught in a ברייתא:
"His bedding": but not stolen bedding,
phrases.notes: ויקרא 15:5, about the bedding of a זב.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Counters אביי's proof by bringing a parallel ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's reading that the ברייתא of קרבנו must be talking about after יאוש.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If 'his, not stolen' wording proves things about יאוש, the same wording about bedding would have to be explained too. As the next step shows, that explanation works just as well for the קרבן.

steps.title: The stolen item was already finished when it was stolen
steps.stepSummary: The bedding ברייתא cannot be about wool made into bedding, because a change made by an action surely gives ownership. So it must be about stealing ready-made bedding. Likewise the קרבן ברייתא is about stealing an animal that was already a קרבן.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If he stole wool and made it into bedding, does anyone say that changing it by an action does not make it his? So you must say he stole his friend's ready-made bedding. In the same way, the other ברייתא is about stealing his friend's animal that was already a קרבן.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא explains the bedding ברייתא and then uses the same explanation for the קרבן ברייתא. This knocks out אביי's proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that שינוי מעשה gives the thief ownership, so the bedding ברייתא must be about bedding stolen as is. In the same way, the קרבן ברייתא can be about an animal that was already a קרבן when it was stolen. An item that belongs to the Temple does not become the thief's, so the ברייתא proves nothing about יאוש.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? Asking for the exact situation
If you say: offering a possible reading that will be rejected
A physical change made by an action, which gives a thief ownership
So too: applying the same idea to the other case

steps.whatToRemember: רבא shows that 'his, not stolen' can mean the item was stolen already in its finished, holy, or usable form. So אביי's proof about יאוש falls away.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If we say that he stole wool
and made it into bedding,
is there anyone who says
that a change made by an action does not give ownership?
phrases.notes: Everyone agrees it does, so in that case the bedding really would be his.

phrases.english: Rather, what must you say?
That he stole his fellow's bedding;
so too,
he stole his fellow's offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבא's counter-argument by explaining both ברייתות as cases where a finished item was stolen.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects אביי's proof from the ברייתא of קרבנו.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: אביי assumed the ברייתא must be about יאוש. It can instead be about an animal that was already a קרבן, which a thief cannot own no matter what.

steps.title: אביי begins a new challenge from a משנה about hides
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רב יוסף with a משנה. A homeowner's decision to use a hide makes it able to become impure, but a tanner's decision does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי raised a challenge to רב יוסף from a משנה: With hides that belong to a homeowner, his thought makes them able to become impure. With hides that belong to a tanner, his thought does not make them able to become impure.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי opens a new challenge by quoting a משנה about leather. This is the setup: the משנה goes on to a thief and a robber in step 8, and אביי makes his point in step 9.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Leather can become impure only once it counts as a finished item. A homeowner who decides to use a hide as it is makes it finished just by deciding. A tanner sells hides, so his decision is not final and does not count.

keyTerms.meaning: A homeowner, a regular private person
A tanner or leatherworker, who processes hides for sale
Thought: deciding how an item will be used
Makes them able to become impure

steps.confusionAlert: 'מחשבה מטמאתן' does not mean the thought makes the hide impure right now. It means the hide now counts as a finished item that is able to become impure.

phrases.english: Abaye raised an objection to Rav Yosef:
Hides belonging to a homeowner:
thought makes them able to become impure.
But those belonging to a tanner:
thought does not make them able to become impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new challenge using a משנה about hides, after רבא rejected the proof from the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Setup only so far: the משנה shows that a person's decision about how a hide will be used can make it count as a finished item. The point of the challenge comes when the משנה applies this to a גנב and a גזלן (step 8), and אביי draws his conclusion in step 9.

steps.title: The quoted משנה continues: a thief versus a robber
steps.stepSummary: The משנה that אביי quoted goes on. The תנא קמא says a גנב's decision counts for the hides and a גזלן's does not. רבי שמעון reverses it, because the owners have not given up hope.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the hides belong to a thief, his decision makes them able to become impure. If they belong to a robber, his decision does not. רבי שמעון says it is the other way around. The robber's decision makes them able to become impure, and the thief's decision does not, because the owners have not given up hope.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still quoting the משנה that אביי brought against רב יוסף. This sets up the point אביי will make in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both opinions agree that in one case the stealer's decision really counts, the way an owner's decision counts. They only argue about which case it is: the secret thief or the open robber. רבי שמעון's reason shows that the key factor is whether the owners gave up hope (יאוש).

keyTerms.meaning: A thief who steals secretly
A robber who takes openly, by force
The matters are reversed
The owners gave up hope of getting it back

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up גנב and גזלן. A גנב steals secretly, and a גזלן takes openly. The two opinions in the משנה flip which one of them the owners give up on.

phrases.english: Those of a thief – thought makes them able to become impure,
phrases.notes: 'Thought' here is the thief's decision to use the hide as it is, just like the homeowner's decision earlier.

phrases.english: those of a robber – thought does not make them able to become impure.
Rabbi Shimon says: the matters are reversed –
those of a robber, thought makes them able to become impure,
and those of a thief, thought does not make them able to become impure;
because the owners have not given up hope.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה quoted in step 7 as the source for אביי's challenge.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's view that יאוש does not make the stealer the owner
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only an owner's decision counts for the hides, yet the משנה says a stealer's decision counts in a case where the owners gave up hope.

steps.title: So giving up hope makes the stealer the owner
steps.stepSummary: אביי draws his point from the משנה: יאוש makes the stealer the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: And learn from this that יאוש makes the stealer the owner!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי lands his challenge. Since the stealer's decision counts like an owner's decision, יאוש must have made him the owner, which goes against רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It doesn't matter whether we follow the תנא קמא or רבי שמעון. In whichever case the owners gave up hope, the stealer acts like the owner. That suggests יאוש alone transfers ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from this; we can conclude
Giving up hope makes the stealer the owner

phrases.english: And learn from it: giving up hope makes him the owner!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the challenging conclusion from the משנה quoted in steps 7-8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's view that יאוש does not acquire
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The stealer's decision only counts if he owns the hide, and the only thing that changed is the owner's יאוש. So יאוש must give ownership.

steps.title: The case is where the stealer trimmed the hides
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that the משנה is talking about a stealer who trimmed the hides. So an action was done together with the יאוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: What case are we dealing with here? A case where he trimmed them.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף defends himself. He says the משנה is not about יאוש alone, because the stealer also trimmed the leather.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer limits the משנה to a specific case. Trimming is a small physical act. Together with the owner's יאוש, it makes the stealer the owner. So the משנה does not prove that יאוש by itself is enough.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source to a specific case)
Trimmed, cut the edges

phrases.english: He said to him: here, with what are we dealing –
for example, where he trimmed them.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the משנה is about hides that were trimmed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The stealer acquired the hides through יאוש alone.
steps.terutzMaskana: The stealer acquired through יאוש plus the act of trimming, so יאוש alone may still not acquire.

steps.title: A table-top cover does not need trimming
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר רב חנן objects that the משנה is about a leather table-top cover, which needs no trimming. So trimming cannot be what made the difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר רב חנן challenges this: But wasn't the משנה taught here about a table-top cover? And a table-top cover doesn't need trimming!
steps.whatsHappening: A new אמורא, רבה בר רב חנן, attacks רב יוסף's answer. The משנה is about a type of leather that is never trimmed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a table-top cover doesn't need trimming, then cutting it is not a real change. It cannot help make the stealer the owner. So the trimming answer seems to fall apart, and the question of יאוש comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: Challenges it (an objection to an answer just given)
A leather table-top cover
Trimming

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַבָּה בַּר רַב חָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Rav Ḥanan challenges it:
But didn't they teach here about a table-top cover,
and a table-top cover does not need trimming!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַבָּה בַּר רַב חָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רב יוסף's answer from step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's claim that the משנה is about hides that were trimmed
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Trimming only matters if it is a real change. A table-top cover never needs trimming, so trimming it changes nothing and cannot explain the ownership.

steps.title: Proof that the table-top cover needs no more work
steps.stepSummary: A משנה in כלים shows that the leather table-top cover (עיצבא) is the one item that can become impure just by a decision, even though work is still missing.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: whenever no work is missing, a decision makes the item able to become impure. When work is still missing, a decision does not, except for the leather table-top cover.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the source for רבה בר רב חנן's claim in step 11. The משנה shows the leather table-top cover counts as finished even before it is trimmed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, if an item still needs work, deciding to use it does nothing. The table-top cover is the exception, because people do not mind its rough edges. So the משנה's case needed no trimming, and רב יוסף's answer about trimming falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: Work still missing before the item is finished
A decision or intention to use the item as it is
Makes it able to become impure
A leather cover for a table-top

phrases.aramaic: דִּתְנַן: כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁאֵין חֶסְרוֹן מְלָאכָה –
phrases.english: As we learned: wherever no work is lacking –
a decision makes it able to become impure;
where work is still lacking –
a decision does not make it able to become impure;
except for the leather table-top cover.
phrases.notes: This exception is the very case the משנה in step 7 was talking about, so no trimming was needed there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the objection in step 11.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that the משנה's case (the table-top cover) needs no trimming.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משנה in כלים: a decision counts for unfinished items only in the case of the עיצבא.

steps.title: רבא reports רב יוסף's answer: a change in name counts like a physical change
steps.stepSummary: רבא reports רב יוסף's final answer: a change in name works like a change made by action.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: רבה pressed רב יוסף with this question for twenty-two years. It was not solved until רב יוסף became head of the yeshiva and solved it: a change in name is like a change made by action.
steps.whatsHappening: The trimming answer failed, so the גמרא gives a brand-new answer. A new name for the hide counts as a real change.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was why the stealer of the hides becomes the owner if יאוש alone is not enough. The new answer is that יאוש here comes together with a change in name, and a change in name counts like a physical change. So there is still no proof that יאוש alone transfers ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: A change in the item's name
A physical change made by an action
It was solved
At the head (as head of the yeshiva)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a new rule, that a name change can count like a physical change. The rest of the section tests that rule.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מִילְּתָא קְשִׁי בַּהּ רַבָּה לְרַב יוֹסֵף
phrases.english: Rabba raised this difficulty against Rav Yosef
for twenty-two years,

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אִיפַּרְקָה עַד דְּיָתֵיב רַב יוֹסֵף בְּרֵישָׁא,
phrases.english: and it was not solved until Rav Yosef sat as head,
and he solved it:
a change in name is like a change made by action.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the failed trimming answer of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New legal rule that explains the case another way
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The stealer became the owner of the hides through יאוש alone.
steps.terutzMaskana: He became the owner because the hides also changed their name, which counts like a physical change.

steps.title: Why does a physical change work?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the reason is behind a physical change making the stealer the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason a physical change works?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a physical change works. This is setting up the next step, which will show that a name change has the same reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To prove a name change is like a physical change, we first need the reason a physical change works. Then we can check whether that reason fits a name change too.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?

phrases.english: A change by action, what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind רב יוסף's comparison in step 13.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The underlying reason that a physical change gives the stealer ownership.

steps.title: Both changes give the item a new identity
steps.stepSummary: Wood became vessels, and a hide became a table-top cover. Each one is now a new thing with a new name.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, at first it was wood and now it is vessels. A change in name is the same: at first they called it a hide, and now they call it a table-top cover.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question. A physical change works because the item turned into something new, and a name change does the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What matters is that the item now has a new identity. Wood made into vessels is no longer 'wood'. A hide used as a table-top cover is no longer called a 'hide', so it counts as changed too.

keyTerms.meaning: At first, originally
Now
A hide
A leather table-top cover

steps.whatToRemember: רב יוסף's answer: a new name means a new identity, just like a physical change. So the stealer of the hides owned them through יאוש plus a change, not through יאוש alone.

phrases.english: there, at first it was wood,
phrases.notes: 'There' means the case of someone who stole wood and made it into vessels, where a physical change makes the stealer the owner.

phrases.english: now it is vessels;
a change in name is the same –
at first they called it a 'hide',
and now a 'table-top cover'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14 and backs up the rule of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A physical change works because the item becomes something new. A change in name also makes it something new.

steps.title: Challenge from the stolen beam built into a building
steps.stepSummary: A beam changes its name once it is built in, yet the owner gets its value only because of a special enactment for people who repent.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what about a beam, where the name changes, since at first it is called a 'beam' and now a 'rafter'? And we learned: about a stolen beam that he built into a large building, the owner takes its value, because of the enactment for those who repent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new rule with a case where the name changed but the change did not seem to make the stealer the owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a name change made the stealer the owner, he would simply owe money by basic law. But the משנה says he pays money only because of a special enactment for those who repent. That suggests that by basic law he would have to give back the beam itself, so the name change did not make him the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: A beam
A beam (before it is built in)
A rafter (once it is part of the roof)
A large building
An enactment to make it easier for people to repent

steps.confusionAlert: The problem is not that the owner gets money. The problem is that the משנה needs a special enactment to say so, which suggests a name change alone would not have done it.

phrases.english: But what about a beam –
where there is a change in name,
since at first it is a 'beam'
and now a 'rafter';
and we learned: about a stolen beam
that he built into a large building,
that the owner takes its value,
because of the enactment for those who repent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the rule from steps 13 and 15 that a name change counts like a physical change.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's rule that שינוי השם counts like שינוי מעשה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The beam changes its name, yet paying money instead of returning it needs a special enactment. So the name change alone did not make the stealer the owner.

steps.title: The only reason is the enactment for those who repent
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its challenge. In the beam case, the stealer keeps the beam only because of תקנת השבים, not because the beam's change of name made it his.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason is only because of the enactment made for people who repent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is driving home the challenge from Step 16. It says the stealer keeps the built-in beam only because of a special enactment, and not because of any change in name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If שינוי השם really made the stealer the owner, the חכמים would not have needed a special enactment to let him pay money instead of returning the beam. Since they did need תקנת השבים, the plain rule must be that a change in name does not transfer ownership. That goes straight against רב יוסף's answer in Step 13.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason. Here it means "the only reason"
Because of
An enactment or rule set up by the חכמים
Those who repent and want to return what they stole

steps.whatToRemember: The beam case shows a new name, yet the stealer keeps it only because of תקנת השבים. That suggests שינוי השם alone does not make him the owner.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the beam has no new name. It agrees the name changed. It is pointing out that the name change was not enough, so a special enactment had to step in.
steps.whyThisMatters: This puts רב יוסף's rule that שינוי השם works like שינוי מעשה in real danger. The גמרא now needs an answer for the beam case.

phrases.english: The reason is because of the enactment for those who repent,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge of Step 16 by stating its key inference: the stealer's right to keep the beam comes only from תקנת השבים.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יוסף's rule (Step 13) that שינוי השם acquires like שינוי מעשה, along with the reasoning of Step 15 that a new name makes a new item.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A built-in beam has a new name. If a new name made the stealer the owner, no enactment would be needed. Since the משנה relies on תקנת השבים, the plain rule must be that a change in name alone does not acquire.
